Effective sample size.long:
A statistical test treats every observation as a fresh piece of information. Effective sample size is the number of genuinely independent observations hiding inside a dataset, and in trading it is almost always smaller than the headline count. Two hundred trades taken during one trending quarter are not two hundred pieces of evidence; they are one market condition sampled two hundred times.

The shrinkage happens mechanically through dependence. Positively autocorrelated observations share information, so each new one adds less than a full observation's worth. Overlapping return windows, trades clustered in a single regime, and strategies holding many correlated positions all inflate the nominal count while leaving the effective count nearly unchanged.

Every significance calculation — p-values, confidence intervals, standard errors — quietly assumes independence. Feed it a nominal count of a thousand when the effective count is sixty and it will report certainty the data does not contain.

Where people get fooled: the trade log looks long, so the conclusion feels solid. But a backtest whose trades all lean on the same few market episodes has the evidential weight of a handful of observations, and the impressive statistics computed from it are precision applied to noise.
Effective sample size.usage: Used to deflate the apparent weight of evidence in a backtest before trusting its statistics — the question asked is how many independent bets the record contains, not how many rows the trade log has.

Overlapping returns.long:
Overlapping returns are multi-period returns sampled more often than the period itself — twelve-month returns computed every month, or five-day returns computed daily. Adjacent observations then share almost all of their underlying data: this month's twelve-month return and next month's differ by only two months out of twelve.

The overlap manufactures autocorrelation that has nothing to do with the market. Because neighbouring observations are mostly the same data, the series looks smooth and persistent by construction, and any regression run on it sees far more observations than genuinely exist. Standard errors computed the ordinary way come out too small, and t-statistics too large.

The honest fixes are to sample non-overlapping windows, which shrinks the dataset to its true size, or to keep the overlap and correct the standard errors with methods built for dependent data, such as Newey-West adjustments. Either way the apparent precision drops, which is the point.

Where people get fooled: a predictor of annual returns tested on monthly overlapping windows can look decisively significant while containing only a handful of independent yearly observations. The result is not evidence about markets; it is the arithmetic of counting the same year twelve times.
Overlapping returns.usage: Comes up whenever a signal is evaluated against returns longer than the sampling interval; the craft is either to use non-overlapping windows or to correct the standard errors, and to distrust any t-statistic that did neither.

Block bootstrap.long:
The ordinary bootstrap builds confidence intervals by resampling individual observations with replacement, which silently assumes each observation is independent. Market returns are not: volatility arrives in clusters, and quiet days follow quiet days. Resampling single days shuffles that structure away and produces synthetic histories better behaved than anything the market has ever printed.

The block bootstrap fixes this by resampling contiguous blocks of the series instead of single points. A block of twenty consecutive days carries its own volatility cluster with it, so the resampled series retains the local dependence of the original. Variants let the block length vary randomly so the splice points are less artificial.

The awkward part is choosing block length. Too short and dependence is destroyed anyway; too long and there are too few distinct blocks to resample meaningfully. There is no universally right answer, only a length long enough to span the dependence that matters for the statistic being estimated.

Where people get fooled: an independent-draws bootstrap on strategy returns yields confidence intervals that are too narrow and drawdown estimates that are too kind, because the resampled worlds never string bad days together the way real markets do.
Block bootstrap.usage: Used when bootstrapping anything computed from a time series — Sharpe intervals, drawdown distributions — where resampling individual observations would destroy the serial dependence the answer depends on.

p-value.long:
A p-value answers one narrow question: if there were genuinely no effect — no edge, pure chance — how probable is data at least as extreme as what was observed? It is a statement about the data given the null hypothesis, not about the hypothesis given the data. A p-value of 0.03 does not mean a three-in-a-hundred chance the strategy is luck, and it certainly does not mean a ninety-seven-in-a-hundred chance it works.

The mechanism that breaks it in trading is repetition. Any single test has a small chance of producing a low p-value from noise alone, so a search across many variants will reliably produce some. The p-value of the best result from a search is not the p-value of a single test; it needed a far higher bar the moment the second variant was tried.

Where people get fooled: the number arrives with an aura of objectivity, but it is only interpretable alongside the count of tests that produced it. A small p-value at the end of a long, unrecorded search is close to worthless — which is why the search itself has to be recorded.
p-value.usage: Read alongside the number of trials that produced it, never alone; in practice the useful question is whether the result clears the significance bar implied by the whole search.

Multiple testing.long:
Every statistical test carries some probability of a false positive. Run one test and that probability is small. Run two hundred and the arrival of at least one impressive-looking result is close to guaranteed, whether or not any real effect exists. Multiple testing is the name for this arithmetic, and it is the central hazard of strategy research, where testing another variant costs nothing.

The mechanism is selection on noise. Each backtest result is truth plus luck. Choose the best of two hundred and you have chosen, in large part, the luckiest — its measured performance is biased upward even if a genuine edge exists somewhere in the batch.

Corrections exist. The Bonferroni correction divides the significance threshold by the number of tests; other procedures control the expected fraction of false discoveries. All of them require knowing how many tests were run, which is why an honest count of trials matters more than any individual result.

Where people get fooled: the failures disappear. A researcher, a forum, or an industry shows only its winners, and the observer judges them as if they were single, isolated tests. Without the denominator, the numerator flatters itself.
Multiple testing.usage: The working discipline is to log every variant tested and raise the evidence bar as the count grows, so the best result of a search is judged against the search, not against zero.

Trial ledger.long:
A trial ledger is a permanent, append-only count of every test ever run against a dataset. Its purpose is to preserve the one number that gives any individual result its meaning: how many attempts it took to find. The best result of ten trials and the best of ten thousand can look identical in isolation; the ledger is what tells them apart.

The mechanism it defends against is quiet accumulation. No single backtest feels like a search, but tests accrete across sessions, ideas, and months, and the false-positive arithmetic compounds with every one. Because the dataset never forgets what has been tried against it, the ledger must not either — which is why failed tests are recorded and never deleted.

In practice the ledger sets the significance bar. As the count rises, the performance threshold a new result must clear to be distinguishable from luck rises with it, mechanically and without exception.

Where people get fooled: memory resets the counter. Each new idea feels like a fresh start, and old failures feel irrelevant to the new hypothesis. Statistically they are not — they were all draws from the same data, and every one of them raised the bar.
Trial ledger.usage: Kept as a running header on research reports so any new result is read against the cumulative number of attempts, not as if it were the first.

Pre-registration.long:
Pre-registration means writing down the hypothesis, the mechanism that might make it true, the success criterion, and the number of variants to be tested — before running anything. The document is a commitment device: once the results exist, they can no longer shape the question.

The mechanism it removes is silent flexibility. After seeing results, a researcher can adjust the metric, the period, the threshold, or the framing until something passes, often without noticing they are doing it. Each adjustment is a fresh draw from the noise. Fixing the analysis in advance closes those degrees of freedom while judgement is still blind.

It also forces the rationale into the open. A hypothesis that cannot be written down with a plausible economic mechanism before testing was never a hypothesis, just a pattern in search of a story.

Where people get fooled: the corruption feels like diligence. Re-examining a failed test, trying a cleaner metric, extending the window — each feels like careful work rather than what it is, which is moving the target after the shot. Pre-registration works precisely because it is written by someone who has not yet seen the answer.
Pre-registration.usage: In practice a short entry — hypothesis, mechanism, pass criterion, variant count — is written before any code runs, and a test that fails its registered criterion is recorded as failed regardless of what else looks interesting in the output.

HARKing.long:
HARKing — hypothesising after the results are known — is finding a pattern first and constructing the explanation second, then presenting the explanation as if it had been the prediction all along. The term comes from psychologist Norbert Kerr, and the practice is endemic wherever data is abundant and stories are cheap.

The mechanism is that the story is selected by the same noise that produced the pattern. If a strategy happens to have worked on Tuesdays, a plausible reason for Tuesday effects can always be found afterwards — markets offer an inexhaustible supply of retrospective mechanisms. The explanation feels like independent support, but it was chosen because it fit, so it adds no evidence at all.

The tell is direction. A genuine rationale exists before the test and could have been embarrassed by it; a HARKed rationale arrives after the result and never fails, because it was reverse-engineered from the answer.

Where people get fooled: hindsight makes every surviving pattern feel explained, and an explained pattern feels real. The fluency of the story is doing the persuading, not the data — which is exactly why rationales have to be written down before results exist.
HARKing.usage: Guarded against by timestamping the hypothesis: if the economic rationale was written after the backtest ran, it counts as decoration, not evidence.

Null result.long:
A null result is a test that found no effect: the strategy did not beat its benchmark, the pattern did not repeat, the edge did not survive costs. In a domain where most tested ideas are noise, this is the usual outcome of honest work — and the informative one.

The mechanism that makes nulls valuable is pruning. Every well-run test that returns nothing removes a branch from the search space, protects capital that would have chased it, and sharpens the prior for the next question. A recorded null also keeps the trial count honest, because the significance of any future winner depends on how many failures preceded it.

A null is not proof of absence. A test with few trades or a weak design can miss a real but small effect; the strength of a null depends on the power of the test that produced it.

Where people get fooled: nulls feel like failure, so they go unrecorded and unshared. The published and remembered record then consists mostly of winners, which makes everything visible look more likely to work than it is. Hiding a null is not neutral; it inflates every result that remains.
Null result.usage: Treated as a deliverable: written up with the same care as a positive result, filed where it can be found, and counted in the ledger so later results are judged against the full search.

Out-of-sample.long:
Out-of-sample data is data that played no role in developing a strategy — not in choosing the rules, not in tuning the parameters, not in deciding which variants to keep. Its value comes entirely from that innocence: it is the only data that can measure how the strategy behaves on information it has never met.

The mechanism is contamination. Any dataset used during development leaks into the strategy, because every decision — keep this rule, drop that one — is partly a response to that data's noise. In-sample performance therefore mixes genuine edge with memorised accident, in unknown proportions. Fresh data contains none of the memorised part, so the gap between in-sample and out-of-sample results is a direct reading of how much was accident.

The innocence is spent on first use. Look at out-of-sample results, adjust the strategy, and test again, and the data has become in-sample for the revised version. Honest research treats each hold-out set as usable once.

Where people get fooled: the quiet second look. Checking the hold-out mid-development, then iterating, preserves the label while destroying the thing the label stood for.
Out-of-sample.usage: Reported first and ranked on, with in-sample figures shown as secondary context; a large in-sample versus out-of-sample gap is read as overfitting until proven otherwise.

Purged cross-validation.long:
Cross-validation estimates how a model performs on unseen data by training on some folds and testing on the rest. The standard version assumes observations are independent, and financial data breaks that assumption in a specific way: a label often spans time. A trade opened on Monday and closed on Friday overlaps every day between them.

When folds are cut from a time series, training observations near the boundary can share their label window with test observations. The model is then trained on near-copies of the data it will be tested on, and the score measures memorisation rather than generalisation. Purging fixes this mechanically: any training observation whose label overlaps the test fold in time is removed before fitting.

The technique is associated with Marcos López de Prado's work on financial machine learning, and is usually paired with an embargo that drops a further buffer of data after the test window to absorb serial correlation.

Where people get fooled: unpurged cross-validation fails silently. The scores come out excellent, the pipeline looks rigorous, and the leakage only reveals itself when the model meets genuinely unseen data and the performance is gone.
Purged cross-validation.usage: Applied whenever cross-validating anything trained on time-series data with labels that span time; the check is whether any training label overlaps the test window at all.

Embargo.long:
An embargo is a buffer of data dropped from training immediately after a test window in cross-validation. Purging removes training observations whose labels overlap the test fold; the embargo goes further and discards a stretch of observations that merely follow it.

The reason is serial correlation. Markets carry information forward in time — volatility clusters, positions unwind over days, reactions echo. An observation shortly after the test window is therefore partly a function of what happened inside it, and training on that observation hands the model a compressed summary of the test data. No label overlap is needed for the leak; adjacency is enough.

The embargo length is a judgement about how long dependence persists. Too short and leakage survives; too long and usable data is wasted. Since dependence in financial series fades gradually rather than stopping cleanly, the choice is a conservative estimate, not a calculation.

Where people get fooled: leakage this subtle never announces itself. It shows up only as validation scores slightly better than the strategy deserves — which is the most dangerous kind of error, because it flatters exactly the results being trusted.
Embargo.usage: Set alongside purging in any time-series cross-validation, sized to the horizon over which returns and volatility remain correlated rather than to a standard number.

Probability of backtest overfitting.long:
Probability of backtest overfitting asks a blunt question of a strategy search: how often does the configuration that looked best in-sample go on to underperform the median configuration out-of-sample? If choosing the in-sample winner is no better than choosing at random, the search discovered nothing.

The mechanics come from combinatorial resampling. The performance history is split into many different train-test partitions; in each, the best in-sample configuration is identified and its out-of-sample rank recorded. The fraction of partitions where the winner lands in the bottom half is the estimate. The framework comes from work by Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado and Zhu.

What makes it useful is that it evaluates the selection process rather than any single backtest. A search can consist of individually reasonable tests and still be almost certain to hand back noise, because picking the maximum of many noisy results is itself the overfitting mechanism.

Where people get fooled: the measure only sees the trials it is given. A search that was quietly wider than the recorded one — variants tried and abandoned, ideas tweaked before formal testing — produces a flattering number that audits the paperwork, not the process.
Probability of backtest overfitting.usage: Run on the full set of configurations from a strategy search as a health check on the selection process itself, before any attention is paid to the winning variant's statistics.

White's Reality Check.long:
White's Reality Check, from econometrician Halbert White in 2000, is a formal test of whether the best strategy found in a search genuinely beats a benchmark, after accounting for the entire search that found it. It was among the first methods to price in data snooping directly rather than treating each strategy as an isolated hypothesis.

The mechanism is a bootstrap of the maximum. Under the null that no strategy has an edge, resampling the performance data many times shows how large the best result of the whole universe would typically be by luck alone. The real winner is then compared against that distribution of best-case flukes, not against zero. Beating zero is easy for the luckiest of hundreds; beating the luckiest of hundreds is the actual claim.

Where people get fooled: the test is only as honest as the universe fed into it. Run it on the final shortlist of ten survivors, rather than the hundreds of variants actually tried, and the snooping bias it exists to remove walks straight back in through the definition of the search.
White's Reality Check.usage: Applied to the complete set of strategies tested against a dataset — including abandoned ones — to ask whether the best of them clears the bar set by luck across the whole search.

Monte Carlo permutation.long:
A Monte Carlo permutation test asks what a strategy's result would look like if its timing contained no information. The link between signals and outcomes is deliberately broken — entry dates shuffled, the signal series permuted against the return series — many thousands of times, and the strategy's metric is recomputed in each scrambled world.

The mechanism is that permutation destroys skill while preserving everything else. The scrambled versions trade the same market, with the same return distribution, the same frequency, and the same holding behaviour; the only thing removed is the alignment between decisions and outcomes. The spread of scrambled results is therefore the distribution of pure luck, and the real result's position within it says how unusual the timing actually was.

Where people get fooled: the scrambling has to preserve the market's structure to be a fair control. A permutation scheme that destroys volatility clustering or serial dependence produces a luck distribution tamer than reality, which makes an ordinary result look exceptional. The test then flatters precisely the strategies it was built to expose.
Monte Carlo permutation.usage: Used to place a backtest result inside the distribution of what chance alone produces on the same market, with the permutation scheme chosen to preserve the return series' dependence structure.

Random trader benchmark.long:
A random trader benchmark is a control group for a strategy: a simulated trader that enters at random but matches the strategy's market, trade frequency, holding period, and costs. Run thousands of them and the output is a distribution of outcomes achievable with no skill whatsoever.

The mechanism it isolates is the free ride. Any long strategy in a rising market collects drift it did nothing to earn; any strategy in a calm regime collects the absence of disasters. Random traders collect exactly the same gifts, so the part of a strategy's performance that clears the random cloud is the part attributable to its decisions rather than its environment.

It complements buy-and-hold as a control. Buy-and-hold asks whether trading was worth doing at all; the random trader asks whether the specific entries and exits contained information beyond their frequency and duration.

Where people get fooled: profitability feels like proof. In a market that rose, most random long traders were profitable too — a strategy sitting comfortably inside the random distribution has demonstrated nothing except that it was present.
Random trader benchmark.usage: Reported above strategy results as a standing control, with a strategy's outcome read as its position within the random distribution rather than as a raw number.

Selection bias.long:
Selection bias is what happens when the sample being studied was filtered by the outcome being measured. The funds with visible track records are the ones that survived; the strategies that get published are the ones that worked; the traders heard from are the ones still solvent. The filter creates the pattern before any analysis begins.

The mechanism is invisible subtraction. Nothing about the surviving data looks wrong — it is clean, complete, and internally consistent. What is missing is the population it was drawn from: the failed funds, the abandoned strategies, the quiet losers. Averages computed on survivors are averages of the lucky tail, and they overstate what a new entrant should expect.

In backtesting it appears as survivorship in the asset universe, where delisted instruments are missing from the data, as cherry-picked date ranges, and — most commonly — as reporting only the variants that passed.

Where people get fooled: the bias cannot be seen from inside the sample. No amount of scrutiny of the surviving data reveals what was removed; the only defence is asking, before analysing anything, how this sample came to be in front of you.
Selection bias.usage: Handled at the design stage by asking what filter produced the dataset — survivorship-free universes, full date ranges, complete search logs — because no statistical correction fixes it afterwards.

Regression to the mean.long:
When an outcome is part skill and part luck, extreme results are extreme partly because the luck ran one way. Luck does not persist, so the next measurement tends to fall back towards the average — with no change in the underlying skill at all. That drift is regression to the mean, and it is arithmetic, not a force.

The mechanism follows from selection. Pick the best quarter, the hottest fund, the top-ranked strategy variant, and the pick is conditioned on good luck as much as good process. The luck component resets on the next draw; the skill component carries over. The noisier the measurement, the larger the fallback.

It is not the gambler's fallacy in reverse. Nothing corrects or compensates; independent draws simply stop including yesterday's luck.

Where people get fooled: the fallback gets a story. A strategy that shone and then faded is described as broken, crowded, or arbitraged away, when often nothing changed except that the luck in the original measurement was never going to repeat. The same error runs forwards: allocating to last year's winner is largely allocating to last year's luck.
Regression to the mean.usage: Applied when interpreting any performance ranking or hot streak: the expected follow-up to an extreme result is a mediocre one, and the size of the fallback is a clue to how noisy the original measurement was.

Law of large numbers.long:
The law of large numbers says the average of many independent draws converges towards the true expectation as the number of draws grows. A trading edge, if one exists, is a small positive expectation buried in enormous per-trade variance; the law is the reason it can only be seen across many trades, never in a handful.

The mechanism is dilution. Each trade's luck is as large as ever, but averaged over more trades its contribution shrinks, while the expectation's contribution stays fixed. Nothing pushes results back on course after a bad run — the run is simply outweighed. The law compensates nothing; it dilutes.

Convergence has conditions. The draws must be independent and the expectation stable — assumptions markets bend, through clustered volatility, regime change, and fat tails. Dependence slows convergence, sometimes drastically, so the honest trade count needed to see an edge is larger than the naive arithmetic suggests.

Where people get fooled: in both directions. Thirty trades are read as destiny when they are mostly variance, and losing streaks are expected to self-correct because results are 'due' — the gambler's fallacy, which is this law misread as a force.
Law of large numbers.usage: The working consequence is a floor on evidence: judgements about expectancy are deferred until the trade count is large enough that variance no longer dominates, and longer still when trades are correlated.

Fat tails.long:
Market returns produce extreme moves far more often than a normal distribution predicts. That excess weight in the extremes is what fat tails means, and it is a measured property of essentially every liquid market, not a rare pathology.

The mechanism is that returns are not the sum of many small independent influences, which is the condition that produces normality. Volatility clusters, so large moves breed large moves; leverage unwinds force selling into falling prices; liquidity withdraws precisely when it is most needed. Each feedback loop fattens the tails beyond what independent noise could produce.

The practical consequence is that standard deviation understates risk. Sigma-counting fails: moves a normal table calls once-in-millennia events arrive within single careers. A large share of a market's long-run return often accrues on a small number of extreme days, so averages conceal where the action actually is.

Where people get fooled: models calibrated on calm stretches of data inherit thin tails, because the sample contained no disaster. The risk numbers look precise right up until the distribution shows what its tails hold — the absence of an extreme event in a backtest window is not evidence that one is not coming.
Fat tails.usage: Accounted for by measuring kurtosis and tail behaviour directly, sizing positions against extreme scenarios rather than standard deviations, and distrusting any risk figure derived from a normality assumption.

Tail risk.long:
Tail risk is exposure to rare, large losses — the outcomes living in the far left of the return distribution. Its defining feature is asymmetry of visibility: the exposure can exist for years while producing nothing but steady gains, because the event that reveals it is rare by definition.

The mechanism behind the most seductive versions is implicit insurance. Strategies that sell options, harvest carry, or provide liquidity earn a small regular premium in exchange for absorbing a large loss when conditions break. The premium arrives every month; the loss arrives once a decade. Any sample that lacks the event shows only the income, so the strategy appears both profitable and safe.

Backtests inherit the same blindness. A window that happens to contain no crisis prices the insurance as free money, and the standard metrics — Sharpe, expectancy, average drawdown — are all computed on the gain side of an unobserved cliff.

Where people get fooled: smoothness reads as safety. A placid equity curve is treated as evidence of low risk, when for this class of strategy it is exactly what the dangerous version looks like before the event.
Tail risk.usage: Probed by asking what the strategy implicitly sells — what scenario would produce its worst day — and by stress-testing against events absent from the sample, since the historical record of a tail-selling strategy is structurally flattering.

Autocorrelation.long:
Autocorrelation is the correlation of a series with a lagged copy of itself — the degree to which today's value carries information about tomorrow's. In liquid markets, raw returns show little of it, because any strong, simple dependence would be traded away. Volatility, by contrast, is heavily autocorrelated: turbulent days cluster.

It also appears where construction guarantees it. Cumulative equity curves, rolling averages, and overlapping return windows are all built from shared underlying data, so successive values move together mechanically. Smoothness and apparent trend in such series is often an artefact of the arithmetic, not a property of the strategy.

Statistically, positive autocorrelation shrinks the effective sample size: correlated observations share information, so a thousand of them may carry the evidence of a hundred. Tests that assume independence — most default standard errors and intervals — come out overconfident on autocorrelated data.

Where people get fooled: the eye reads persistence as meaning. Runs in an equity curve, streaks in monthly results, and trends in rolling Sharpe all look like signal, but cumulated noise autocorrelates by construction and produces convincing streaks with nothing behind them.
Autocorrelation.usage: Checked before trusting any statistic computed on a series — the lag structure determines how much to shrink the effective sample size and whether default standard errors can be believed.

Noise floor.long:
The noise floor is the level of measured performance that a search would produce by chance alone. It is not zero. Test one random strategy and its expected result is nothing; test five hundred and the best of them will look genuinely good, because the maximum of many noisy draws sits well above the average draw.

The floor rises mechanically with the size of the search. Every additional variant, parameter setting, or re-examined idea adds another draw, and the expected best-of-search climbs. This is why a result can only be judged against the search that produced it: the same performance that would be remarkable as a single pre-registered test can sit comfortably below the floor of a wide sweep.

Estimating the floor is what permutation tests, random trader benchmarks, and reality-check procedures exist for — they simulate the searching-without-skill process and report what its winners look like.

Where people get fooled: results are compared against zero because zero is easy. The honest comparison is against the best that luck achieves across the whole search, a bar that most visible winners were never tested against.
Noise floor.usage: Estimated for the actual search size before interpreting its best result; anything that fails to clear the floor is filed as noise regardless of how it looks in isolation.

Confidence interval.long:
A confidence interval is a range produced by a procedure with a known long-run property: applied across many repeated experiments, intervals built this way capture the true value a stated fraction of the time. The ninety-five in a ninety-five per cent interval describes the procedure's reliability over repetitions — not a probability that the truth lies inside this particular interval.

Its practical value in trading is honesty about width. A backtest reports a point estimate — an expectancy, a Sharpe — that looks precise, while the interval around it, computed from a limited and noisy trade history, is usually wide enough to be humbling. For modest trade counts, the honest interval around most performance metrics includes zero.

Width depends on assumptions. Intervals computed under independence come out too narrow on dependent data, because correlated observations carry less information than their count suggests; bootstrap methods that respect the dependence structure give wider, more truthful ranges.

Where people get fooled: the point estimate travels and the interval stays home. A strategy whose Sharpe interval spans zero gets reported, remembered, and compared by the point estimate alone, as if the width were a footnote rather than the finding.
Confidence interval.usage: Quoted alongside any headline performance metric to show how much the data actually pins down; an interval spanning zero is read as not yet distinguishable from nothing.

Standard deviation.long:
Standard deviation measures the typical spread of outcomes around their average, computed by squaring deviations, averaging, and taking the root. In finance it is the conventional definition of volatility and the denominator of the Sharpe ratio, which makes it the default unit of risk almost everywhere.

The squaring step gives it a character worth knowing: large deviations dominate the calculation, and upside surprises count exactly as much as downside ones. It summarises a distribution well when that distribution is roughly symmetric and thin-tailed — conditions market returns fail. On fat-tailed data the standard deviation is unstable, dragged around by whichever extremes the sample happens to include.

Annualisation adds another assumption. Scaling daily volatility by the square root of time is only valid when returns are independent across days; autocorrelation and volatility clustering bend that arithmetic, so annualised figures inherit an error most users never see.

Where people get fooled: low standard deviation is read as low risk. Strategies with tail exposure are engineered, deliberately or not, to score well on it — steady small gains, rare large losses — so the measure is most flattering precisely where it is most wrong.
Standard deviation.usage: Used as the common currency for comparing variability, with the caveats attached: check the tails, check the autocorrelation, and treat annualised figures as approximations.

Volatility clustering.long:
Volatility clustering is the observation that large price moves tend to be followed by large moves, and calm by calm. The direction of tomorrow's move is close to unpredictable, but its likely size is not — turbulence arrives in episodes, not as isolated days.

The mechanics are self-reinforcing. News that moves prices tends to arrive in connected streams as a situation develops. Risk management responds to volatility with deleveraging, and forced selling creates further movement. Options hedging flows scale with recent movement. Each channel converts today's turbulence into tomorrow's, producing the clusters visible in every liquid market's history.

Statistically, clustering means returns are not independent even when they are uncorrelated. Independence-based tools quietly break: square-root-of-time annualisation, ordinary bootstraps, and permutation schemes that shuffle single days all produce synthetic worlds calmer than reality, flattering whatever is tested against them.

Where people get fooled: forecastable volatility gets mistaken for forecastable returns. Knowing tomorrow is likely to be turbulent says little about its sign — clustering is one of the most solid regularities in markets precisely because knowing about it does not, by itself, hand anyone a directional edge.
Volatility clustering.usage: Respected in testing rather than traded on: resampling and simulation methods are chosen to preserve clustering, and risk estimates are allowed to vary with the current regime rather than assumed constant.

Effect size.long:
Effect size is the magnitude of an effect — how big, in real units — as distinct from how detectable it is. For a trading strategy the natural effect size is expectancy: what a trade earns on average, after costs, in currency or basis points. A p-value says whether an effect is distinguishable from zero; the effect size says whether it matters.

The two separate cleanly because detectability is purchasable with data. Given enough trades, an edge too small to cover the spread will still register as statistically significant, because significance measures the ratio of effect to sampling noise, and sampling noise shrinks as observations accumulate. Statistical significance and economic significance are different questions with different answers.

Where people get fooled: significance is reported and magnitude is not. A strategy can be genuinely, provably better than random and still be worthless after costs — a real effect of trivial size. The reverse error also appears: a large measured effect from a tiny sample gets trusted, when the measurement is mostly noise wearing the costume of magnitude.
Effect size.usage: Stated in after-cost units alongside any significance claim, so the question of whether an effect is real never substitutes for the question of whether it is big enough to survive trading.

Power.long:
Power is the probability that a test detects an effect of a given size when the effect genuinely exists. It rises with sample size and effect size and falls with noise. Trading sits at the unfavourable corner: real edges, where they exist, are small relative to the per-trade variance around them, so tests built on realistic trade counts are chronically underpowered.

Low power produces two failures, one obvious and one subtle. The obvious one is missing real effects — a genuine edge fails the test because the sample could never have revealed it. The subtle one is the winner's curse: when an underpowered test does return a significant result, the measured effect must have been inflated by luck to clear the bar, so the estimate is biased upward, sometimes severely.

Where people get fooled: a failed test is read as proof of no edge, when the honest reading is that the test could not have seen an edge of plausible size — a power calculation would have said so in advance. Meanwhile the effects that do pass underpowered tests get taken at face value, which is precisely when they should be shrunk.
Power.usage: Estimated before testing — given a plausible effect size and the available trades, could this test see anything? — and used afterwards to temper both null results and the size of any effect that passed.

Sample effect size.long:
The sample effect size is the effect as measured in the data at hand — the backtest's expectancy, the observed Sharpe — as opposed to the true underlying effect. The two differ by sampling error, and in trading data the sampling error is routinely larger than any plausible true effect.

The bias enters through selection. Results become visible by being large: the best variant of a search, the test that passed, the strategy that earned a write-up. Conditioning on largeness means conditioning on favourable noise, so the visible sample effect is the true effect plus luck that will not repeat. The wider the search and the noisier the data, the larger the flattery.

This is regression to the mean applied to research: the honest forecast for live performance is the sample estimate shrunk towards zero, with more shrinkage for smaller samples and wider searches.

Where people get fooled: expectations are sized off the backtest number as if it were the truth rather than the luckiest measurement of it. Live results then look like decay or breakage, when they are often just the effect returning to its actual size.
Sample effect size.usage: Treated as an upper bound rather than an estimate whenever the result was selected for being good; planning assumes a shrunken version, and live performance is judged against that.

Effective breadth.long:
Effective breadth is the number of genuinely independent bets a strategy or portfolio makes, as opposed to the nominal count of positions or signals. Grinold's fundamental law of active management ties performance to skill multiplied by the square root of breadth — but the breadth that counts is the independent kind, and independence is scarce.

Correlation collapses it mechanically. Fifty positions driven by one underlying factor are, informationally, close to a single bet expressed fifty times: when the factor moves, they move together, and the diversification implied by the count never materialises. The same arithmetic applies to research — twenty parameterisations of one idea, trading the same signal on the same market, contribute the statistical evidence of roughly one.

Where people get fooled: breadth is counted in rows. A portfolio of many holdings, a firm running many strategies, a backtest with many trades — each looks diversified by count while the correlation structure quietly reduces it to a handful of real bets. The claimed benefits, whether smoother returns or stronger evidence, scale with the effective number, and the effective number is the one nobody computes.
Effective breadth.usage: Estimated from the correlation structure before crediting any diversification or evidence claim — the question is how many independent return streams actually exist, not how many line items.

Backtest overfitting by iteration.long:
No single backtest overfits much. The damage is done by the loop: run a test, look at the results, adjust the idea, run again. Each look transfers a little information from the dataset into the researcher, and each adjustment writes it into the strategy. After enough cycles the rules encode the sample's accidents, and the process never contained a step that felt like cheating.

The mechanism is that the researcher becomes the overfitting algorithm. A parameter sweep at least announces its size; iteration hides its trial count inside judgement. Choices about what to try next are conditioned on everything seen so far, so the effective number of trials is far larger than the number of formal runs — and unlike a sweep, it goes unrecorded by default.

The dataset degrades cumulatively. Every iteration spends a little of its ability to say anything fresh, which is why the honest unit of accounting is the total history of contact with the data, not the current experiment.

Where people get fooled: iteration feels like craftsmanship. Refining, polishing, responding to results — the experience is of work improving, while the statistics are of a search widening.
Backtest overfitting by iteration.usage: Contained by pre-registering each cycle as a new trial and logging it, so the ledger reflects the true breadth of the search rather than the flattering count of one idea, refined.

Reporting the whole search.long:
Reporting the whole search means disclosing every variant tested — the failures, the abandoned branches, the near-misses — alongside whatever won. The full count is the denominator that makes the winner interpretable: the best of ten and the best of ten thousand are different objects, and only the report distinguishes them.

The mechanism is the upward bias of maxima. The best result of a search overstates its own true quality by an amount that grows with the search's size. Given the denominator, that bias can be estimated and corrected; without it, no correction is possible even in principle, and the reader is left judging a lottery winner as if it were the average ticket.

The failure mode is passive, not conspiratorial. Failed tests are boring, so they go unwritten; abandoned variants leave no trace; memory compresses a month of tweaking into one remembered idea. The visible record ends up curated by default.

Where people get fooled: everyone else's results arrive pre-filtered. Papers, forums, vendors, and track records show numerators without denominators, and the reader supplies a flattering denominator of one. The habit of reporting one's own full search is also the habit of asking for everyone else's.
Reporting the whole search.usage: Operationalised as a standing rule: the report leads with the trial count, failed variants are listed rather than summarised away, and any result presented without its search is treated as unevaluable.
